Title: Ship fuel shortage looms as refiners strained by war favour other products
Article:
LONDON: A shortage of fuel oil used in ships and power plants looms in the third quarter as refiners increasingly squeezed by wars that have disrupted both crude processing and tanker traffic prioritise output of diesel and other products at their expense.
While crude oil has avoided major price spikes in recent months, refined product prices have soared as strikes damage refineries in Russia and the Middle East and curbs on ship traffic choke flows. China has also cut refining capacity and exports to avoid burning stocks.
Tightening supply threatens to further raise costs for shipowners and power generators already dealing with war-related disruptions. Higher bunker fuel costs could also in turn feed into shipping rates.
Asia will be hardest-hit, as it is most reliant on Gulf flows disrupted by the Iran war, with Singapore, the world's largest bunker hub, importing more than half its nearly 1 million barrels a day of demand, according to import data from Kpler. Consultancy Rystad has a similar outlook.
The deficit is expected to hit 218,000 barrels per day in the third quarter, consultancy Energy Aspects has forecast, the first shortfall it has estimated since the third quarter of 2025, when it was a marginal 6,000 bpd.
"Due to the protracted supply disruption in the Middle East, we expect fuel oil supply to remain critically tight in the third quarter," Rystad analyst Valerie Panopio told Reuters.
Fuel oil joins gasoline, diesel and jet fuel among the refined products struggling to keep up with demand. U.S. diesel prices hit record highs on Friday as renewed OUS-Iran hostilities and Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries increased supply disruptions.
Refiners opting to produce some of those other products to tap fatter profits has meant fuel oil has been hit harder.
Nigeria's 650,000-barrel-per-day Dangote refinery, for example, has ramped up diesel, gasoline and jet fuel exports, while its fuel oil exports have dropped, according to Kpler.
Dangote and other refineries can use fuel oil as feedstock in secondary refining units to make other fuels.
"Record-low gasoline and diesel inventories will incentivise refiners globally to maximise secondary unit runs with more fuel oil feedstock barrels, in turn tightening fuel oil balances," Energy Aspects analyst Royston Huan said.
Gasoline stocks independently held in the Amsterdam-Rotterdam-Antwerp hub hit their lowest level in nearly five years on August 27. US East Coast distillate inventories, which include diesel, fell to a record low in the week to August 28.
PRICE UP 76 PER CENT IN TOP HUB SINGAPORE
Fuel oil storage levels and prices already reflect the pressure.
Stocks are some 30 per cent below three-year seasonal averages in top hubs Singapore, Amsterdam-Rotterdam-Antwerp and Fujairah, data compiled by Reuters shows.
Ships sailing longer routes to avoid key oil chokepoints, the Bab el-Mandeb strait or the Red Sea altogether due to threats by Houthi militants, also increase demand, Panopio noted.
The price of the main shipping fuel, very low sulphur fuel oil, is up 76 per cent since the Iran war started to just under $825 a metric tonne, or $130 a barrel, in Singapore as of September 1, data from bunker price platform ZeroNorth shows.
That outstrips a 40 per cent rise in benchmark Brent crude oil in the same period.
HITS TO RUSSIA, MIDDLE EAST OUTPUT
Ukrainian drone attacks have affected Russia's refinery output, with its fuel oil exports in August hitting a record low of 591,000 bpd, down from an average of over 860,000 bpd in 2025, according to Kpler data going back to 2017.
Middle East fuel oil exports were down by 45 per cent year on year to an average of 447,000 barrels per day in March-August, Kpler data showed.
Refinery outages in the Middle East have included the Al-Zour refinery in Kuwait, a top fuel oil exporter, which has only exported one 26,000 bpd cargo since March versus around 191,000 bpd in January-February, Kpler data showed.

Title: SUV driver arrested after allegedly running red light, fleeing crash
Article:
MIRI: An SUV driver who allegedly ran a red light and crashed into a motorcycle at a traffic junction here on Saturday has been arrested.
District police chief Assistant Commissioner Mohd Farhan Lee Abdullah said the foreign suspect, in his 30s, was arrested with the Brunei-registered Toyota Prado near the Sungai Tujoh border.
He said police received a report on the 8.35pm collision involving the SUV and a motorcycle ridden by a local woman in her 30s.
"Initial investigations found that the SUV allegedly ran a red light before crashing into the motorcycle and fleeing the scene.
"The motorcyclist suffered minor injuries and received treatment at a private clinic. No other vehicles were involved," he said in a statement today.
The incident went viral on social media, sparking outrage over the driver's actions.
Farhan said the suspect and vehicle were taken to the Miri district police headquarters' Traffic Enforcement and Investigation Division for further investigation.
The case is being investigated under Section 43(1) of the Road Transport Act 1987 for careless and inconsiderate driving.
Those with information can contact traffic investigating officer Inspector Mohd Faizul Ab. Rahim at 014-8582582 or 085-430479, or visit the nearest police station.

Title: Samarahan records very unhealthy API reading, 40 areas unhealthy
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: Samarahan in Sarawak was the only area in the country to record a very unhealthy Air Pollutant Index (API) reading of 222 as of 7am today.
Meanwhile, 40 other areas nationwide registered unhealthy API levels.
Data from the Air Pollutant Index Management System (APIMS) portal showed 11 areas in Sarawak recorded unhealthy readings, namely Sarikei (193), Kuching (192), IPD Serian (192), Sri Aman (184), Mukah (182), Sibu (182), Samalaju (180), Bintulu (172), ILP Miri (170), Miri (166), and Limbang (150).
In the Klang Valley, nine areas recorded unhealthy readings above 100, including Johan Setia (184), Shah Alam (166), Batu Muda (163), Putrajaya (163), Cheras (161), Kuala Selangor (158), Petaling Jaya (157), Banting (157), and Klang (156).
In Negri Sembilan, three areas registered unhealthy air quality: Nilai (166), Seremban (163), and Port Dickson (123).
In Melaka, Bukit Rambai recorded 154, followed by Alor Gajah (154) and Melaka City (107).
Unhealthy API levels were also recorded in four areas in Perak, namely Tanjung Malim (160), Seri Manjung (158), Tasek Ipoh (155), and Pegoh Ipoh (145).
In Pahang, the affected areas were Temerloh (153) and Jerantut (152).
In Johor, Segamat and Batu Pahat both recorded readings of 157, followed by Tangkak (153) and Kluang (151).
In Sabah, Kota Kinabalu and Kimanis recorded unhealthy air quality with readings of 153.
Meanwhile, 24 areas nationwide recorded moderate air quality, while two areas registered good readings.
An API reading of zero to 50 indicates good air quality, 51 to 100 moderate, 101 to 200 unhealthy, 201 to 300 very unhealthy, and above 300 hazardous.

Title: Challenging terrain may have delayed six missing hikers, says guide
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: A mountain guide involved in the search-and-rescue (SAR) operation for six missing hikers in Gua Musang believes the group may have been delayed by challenging terrain.
The 34-year-old mountain guide, who requested anonymity, said the group was unlikely to be lost, but likely took longer to navigate the difficult route.
The group entered the forest via Pos Dakoh, Lojing, Gua Musang, and was scheduled to emerge via Pos Kemar in Perak on Sept 3.
"The trek they used for the full expedition involves Mount Gerah, Bilah, and Bieh, known as Trans GBB. It is not a commercial route and is rarely used, perhaps only once or twice a year," he said.
"The route is challenging as it is dense with bamboo and fallen trees, forcing them to blaze new paths, which slows progress. I am confident they are safe, as the two mountain guides accompanying them are highly experienced with the terrain," he added.
Sharing details of the SAR operation, he said he and 12 other mountain guides would trek into the area from 8am today.
"For the first phase, we will enter via Pos Kemar using the Sungai Siput route, moving either as one team or split into two groups. We hope to cross paths with them on their way down, either halfway through or near the exit point," he said.
He added that the team was prepared to remain in the forest for several days with sufficient food supplies, depending on conditions on the ground.
"Basic equipment, including parangs and communication devices like walkie-talkies, are being brought along to assist movement and search operations," he said.
However, he noted that communication would be a major challenge due to the lack of phone signal and walkie-talkie coverage along the route.
"If the victims are in good condition, we will provide initial aid and bring them out. But if assistance like winching is required, we will inform the relevant authorities," he said.
It was earlier reported that
six people, including four family members
and two mountain guides, were feared lost after entering the forest via Pos Dakoh, Lojing, Gua Musang, on Aug 29.
Gua Musang police chief Superintendent Sik Choon Foo said police received a missing persons report from family members in Selangor after the group failed to emerge as scheduled on Sept 3.
He said checks with the Forestry Department indicated the last recorded contact showed the group was already in the Perak forest area before communications were lost.
The group possessed a valid forestry permit and was scheduled to exit via Pos Kemar, Perak. Gua Musang police remain on standby should confirmation arrive that they are in Kelantan territory.
Following the report, Fire and Rescue Department director-general Datuk Seri Nor Hisham Mohammad said
a SAR team was established
to track the group using helicopters starting today.
Nor Hisham added that the operation was being assisted by the mountain guides on the ground to identify and mark the route believed to have been taken by the group.

Title: Two semi-detached houses, Honda Civic damaged in Port Klang fire
Article:
KLANG: Two semi-detached houses and a car were damaged in an early morning fire at Kampung Telok Gong, Port Klang, today.
Selangor Fire and Rescue Department assistant director of operations Ashrul Riezal Asbar said the department received an emergency call regarding the incident at Jalan Telok Gong at 3.01am.
Firefighters arrived at the scene at 3.12am and found the fire involving two semi-detached houses measuring 24ft by 50ft.
[[nid:1527243]]
About 15 per cent of the houses were damaged, while a Honda Civic was 80 per cent burnt.
Photographs from the scene showed flames engulfing the property's front and roof, with thick smoke billowing as firefighters battled the blaze.
Several firefighters were seen directing water jets at the burning structure, while another photograph showed flames visible around the extensively damaged car.
Ashrul said firefighters extinguished the blaze, and no casualties were reported.
A total of 14 firefighters from the Port Klang and Sri Andalas Fire and Rescue stations were deployed to the scene.
The operation involved two Fire Rescue Tender engines, a water tanker, and an Emergency Medical Rescue Services vehicle.

Title: Ringgit opens slightly higher against US dollar
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: The ringgit opened slightly higher against the US dollar on Monday, buoyed by expectations of a potential United States (US) interest rate hike following stronger-than-expected US non-farm payrolls (NFP) data.
At 8 am, the local currency inched up to 4.0415/0500 against the greenback from last Friday's close of 4.0425/0465.
Bank Muamalat Malaysia Bhd chief economist Dr Mohd Afzanizam Abdul Rashid said the higher-than-expected NFP suggests the US Federal Reserve (Fed) is likely to raise its benchmark interest rate at the upcoming Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting on Sept 15-16.

Title: Oil extends gains after US and Iran strike ships
Article:
Reuters
SINGAPORE: Oil prices extended gains on Monday as tit-for-tat strikes between the US and Iran on vessels sailing in the Strait of Hormuz and other areas heightened concerns of a prolonged supply disruption from the Middle East.
Brent crude futures climbed 52 cents, or 0.54 per cent, to US$96.80 a barrel by 2354 GMT while US West Texas Intermediate crude was at US$92.14 a barrel, up 66 cents, or 0.72 per cent.
Brent rose 7.8 per cent last week while WTI gained nearly 10 per cent after the US and Iran resumed attacks and caused a reduction in oil flows through the Hormuz strait where a fifth of the world's oil supply used to transit.
US forces struck three Iranian oil tankers on Saturday, US Central Command said, including one off the coast of Kharg Island, near Iran's key oil export hub.
The navy of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said on Saturday it targeted three oil tankers that were travelling through unauthorized routes in the Strait of Hormuz as well as three additional US vessels in other areas.
The Saturday attacks represented a "major escalation in the maritime conflict", maritime intelligence firm Marisks said.
"Commercial tankers are now being deliberately used as instruments of reciprocal economic pressure, substantially weakening the previous distinction between military confrontation and commercial shipping," it added.
An average of 10 commodity ships transited the Strait of Hormuz per day over the past 10 days, the lowest since May, data from analytics firm Kpler showed on Monday.
A restricted zone will be announced outside the Strait of Hormuz in coming days, Mohsen Rezaei, the secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, said on Sunday, according to state media.
OPEC+ kept ​its oil output policy unchanged for October at a meeting on Sunday, the producer group said in a statement, as it needs to agree new quotas before deciding its next output steps.
A prolonged standoff, punctuated by calibrated military action by the US and Iran, appeared to be the most likely scenario and was likely to delay the path to full recovery of Middle East supply, ANZ analysts said in a note.
"We then expect exports to remain constrained through the rest of 2026, before a gradual reopening late in Q4 2026," they said, adding that a return to pre-war throughput is not expected until late first quarter or early second quarter of 2027.

Title: Australia moves to give users more control over social media algorithms
Article:
SYDNEY: Australians could be given the option of opting out of powerful social media algorithms under new legislation cracking down on big tech, a minister said Monday.
The draft law requiring a "digital duty of care" is expected to be introduced to Australia's parliament this week.
It would require firms like Meta to give users the option of turning off algorithms that tailor recommendations to their personal taste.
"A lot of Australians appreciate the algorithm, both for the enjoyment they get out of it or the utility they get out of it," Communications Minister Anika Wells told national broadcaster ABC.
"A lot of Australians will want to choose the algorithm – but we think that big tech should offer them the choice in the first place, and they should respect that choice."
"We should give Australians more choice over what they should see on their feeds," she said.
Social media firms have long faced scrutiny over their use of allegedly addictive algorithms and stand accused of directing users to sensational or extreme content to keep them scrolling.
Australia implemented legislation barring children from social media platforms in December, part of a world-first crackdown designed to protect children from online bullying and "predatory algorithms."
The UK, France and others have followed suit.
Data last month found that under-16s in Australia were increasing their use of social media apps such as Instagram and TikTok despite the ban.--AFP

Title: US envoys have 'more effective proposals': Ukraine
Article:
KYIV: Washington's envoys have brought new, "more effective" proposals on ending the war with Russia to Kyiv, a senior Ukrainian presidential official told AFP Sunday.
Earlier Sunday, Volodymyr Zelenskyy had said the war with Russia looked likely to continue into the winter.
While both he and the US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner had given upbeat assessments of the talks, neither announced any breakthroughs on ending the conflict.
But the senior Ukrainian official told AFP: "It's not the same as it was before. This one now is more effective. They're still talking. This is actually the most important part."
Witkoff, who is President Donald Trump's business ally, and Kushner, Trump's son-in-law, travelled to Kyiv a day after meeting Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow – the latest of several visits to the city.
Ukraine's rail operator announced their departure from Kyiv in a post on Telegram early Monday, accompanied by a photo of the two envoys' standing under a station sign announcing the "Peace Express."
Sunday's visit to Kyiv was their first to the Ukrainian capital, which has been enduring deadly Russian strikes for more than four years.
Zelenskyy said: "We very much hope that we will be able to reach agreements with our American partners, and we are counting on the support of our European partners if the war continues in winter – and this is how it appears at the moment."
Zelenskyy also said Ukraine would hold talks with the US, France and Germany, but did not elaborate. And he repeated his call that only a meeting between the two leaders could solve territorial issues.
Thanking the US envoys for their visit, Zelenskyy said on X: "The main thing is to achieve peace for Ukraine – a dignified, reliable, and lasting peace. We are directing all our efforts toward this."
- 'ON SAME SIDE' -
Moscow occupies large swathes of eastern and southern Ukraine and the Kremlin told the Americans on Saturday it was feeling "confident" it would advance more.
Moscow has said it wants not just the territories it occupies but the land it claims as Russian to be recognised as its own – terms unacceptable to Kyiv.
Witkoff said both sides would need to compromise, adding: "We think we have the ingredients to get to that place.
"We've had a very meaningful discussion, substantive, important, and we are very encouraged and we look forward to continuing this as long as it takes."
Kushner added: "Hopefully this trip has come out with some new ways to advance forward. I think we've learned a lot from the trip."
Witkoff and Kushner travelled to the region hoping to revive the Trump administration's push for peace in Europe's worst conflict since World War II, after a summer of escalation.
British, French and German representatives attended a separate round of the talks.
Zelenskyy said he was grateful the Europeans were there, adding: "Here we are all on the same side."
Like all visiting officials, the US delegation had arrived by train, with "Peace Express" written on the platform at Kyiv Central Station.
Ukrainian airspace has been closed since Russia launched its invasion in 2022.
Russia and Ukraine vowed not to strike each other's capitals during the US envoys' trip.
- 'SUBSTANTIVE PLANS' -
Moscow's invasion has killed hundreds of thousands of people and displaced millions.
A White House official said in a statement to AFP that in Moscow the envoys had "discussed substantive plans which will be announced in the coming weeks."
Without elaborating, the Kremlin said the Americans had "put forward a number of ideas on possible routes to a settlement."
Putin has repeatedly said Moscow intends to seize the rest of eastern Ukraine, and Russia increased deadly strikes this summer.
Since Putin launched the invasion in February 2022, the war has dragged on with no end in sight.
In Kyiv, few people appeared to believe in a breakthrough.
Nataliia Lipekh, 67, said it was "absolutely necessary (for them) to be here" and to see that "our land is already soaked with this blood and that we need some help."
"At the moment, I have no grounds for hope," said 29-year-old Yaroslav, saying he had seen "far too many of these negotiation processes."--AFP

Title: Miracle rescues lift hopes as Nepal flood search enters 12th day
Article:
KATHMANDU: Nepali rescuers faced challenging conditions on Sunday as search operations after catastrophic floods entered a 12th day, buoyed by the extraordinary rescues of four survivors.
The glacial and mountain collapse on the China-Nepal border killed at least 1,385 people and left more than 5,500 missing across the two countries.
Rescuers found two more people alive on Saturday, joining two saved the day before in what have been described as miraculous tales of survival.
Three of those have been found in hydropower tunnels where the government initially said it believed more than 100 workers could be alive.
"Search and rescue is going on at the tunnels despite geography, adverse weather and lack of connectivity," Energy Minister Biraj Bhakta Shrestha told AFP.
Rescue workers were experiencing "multiple challenges", he said.
The wall of icy water and debris tore through mountain districts on August 26, destroying roads, bridges and other infrastructure.
The United Nations chief in Nepal issued an emotional plea for aid, saying survivors of the catastrophic flooding had seen their lives transformed in just "one to two minutes."
"You lose your home, you lose your livelihood, you lose your loved one and you lose the breadwinner of your family," UN Resident Coordinator Lila Pieters Yahia told AFP in Kathmandu on Sunday.
On Saturday, rescuers pulled a Chinese man alive from deep inside a hydropower tunnel, and a 64-year-old Nepali woman, Chandrika Shrestha, from her mud-covered home.
Prime Minister Balendra Shah said Shrestha's rescue had "given hope to the entire nation."
A day earlier, two Nepali hydropower workers were rescued at the Trishuli 3A tunnel, where searches continue alongside multiple other sites, with at least 12 hydropower projects affected.
Other examples of remarkable fortitude have emerged from Nepal, including Rajendra Dawadi, a school principal who quickly ordered an evacuation as the torrent approached, saving hundreds of students' lives.
"If the information was wrong, we would lose a day of schooling," he told AFP.
"But if it was true, we were going to lose our lives."
- DEATH TOLLS RISE -
Biraj Bhakta Shrestha, the energy minister, said work was continuing to restore electricity in several areas.
"Places that have been unreachable, we've tried to restore power with solar," he told AFP.
Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal has called the disaster a "Himalayan tsunami" and warned reconstruction costs could run into the billions of dollars.
The UN has said the magnitude of the destruction makes delivering aid an immense challenge. It launched a US$50 million appeal to help more than 84,000 people.
With mortuaries overflowing, Nepal has buried hundreds of bodies in mass graves, after taking DNA samples for future identification, according to the police.
Only around 100 bodies have been identified and handed over to families.
Nepal will hold a national day of mourning on Monday, the 13th day since the disaster, in line with a traditional period of mourning in Hindu rituals.
While the exact cause of the glacial collapse is unclear, climate change is accelerating glacial melting worldwide, increasing the risk of such disasters.
In Nepal, rescuers have retrieved 1,342 bodies, while around 4,996 people remain missing, according to the disaster agency.
The death toll from the disaster in Tibet has risen from 31 to 43, Chinese state news agency Xinhua reported on Sunday.
A further 519 people are missing, it said.
Foreign journalists cannot travel freely in China's Tibet Autonomous Region and may only visit as part of strictly controlled trips organised by the authorities.
Chinese media have primarily focused their reporting on the scale of search and rescue operations, and have not broadcast footage showing the reactions of families.
The combined toll is 1,385 dead and more than 5,500 missing, including around 800 foreigners, among them tourists and pilgrims.--AFP
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Nepali woman found alive 10 days after family began mourning her death
Article:
BETRAWATI:  Believing she had perished in Nepal's deadly floods, the family of Chandika Kumari Shrestha started the ritual of mourning the elderly woman's death.
Ten days later, rescuers found her alive inside her collapsed home in the devastated Betrawati village, where she had survived in a narrow pocket of air amid water and mud.
"The four-storey house was swept (away) by the floods and the house was left in the middle of a quicksand. While walking around it, we heard a voice 'save me,'" police officer Mahendra Darnal said.
In a rescue operation on Saturday lasting 45 minutes, Darnal and his team found Shrestha in a confined space and sent her to an army hospital.
"I was in touch with the family and they had started the 11-day mourning period," Darnal said.
Shrestha was among the hundreds missing in Betrawati, an area among the hardest hit by the floods in Nepal and engulfed with white deposits compacted almost like concrete. Crews continue to recover scores of dead bodies.
The town's market and most residential buildings, some as tall as four storeys, were almost completely buried under debris left by a torrent that swept through the valley, part of a disaster that killed more than 1,300 people across Nepal. Thousands remain unaccounted for.
Rescue workers wearing hard hats were seen digging with shovels, while some were crawling through the gaps of collapsed buildings periodically blowing whistles to get the attention of anyone trapped and alive.
Five days earlier, 24 bodies were found in a decomposed state in Betrawati's market area in a building that had contained a small shop, Darnal said.
LOOKING FOR SIGNS OF LIFE
Eleven days since a glacial collapse triggered the devastating floods, close to 5,000 are still missing.
Hundreds of bodies have been swept onto the banks of rivers far from the ravaged Rasuwa district. In Chitwan, hundreds of miles away, several rounds of mass burials have taken place for unidentified and badly decomposed bodies.
Even as hope is beginning to fade, Nepal authorities continue their effort to look for people stuck in tunnels and under the thick deposits of mud that have hardened over buildings.
Since Friday, they have pulled out three people from the tunnels, including a Chinese citizen by the Trishuli river, where more than 900 are believed to be trapped.
Others like Shrestha have survived in extraordinary conditions, including an 8-year-old boy who was also reunited with his mother.--REUTERS

Title: The case for making Malaysia one connected production economy
Article:
IF neighbouring states increasingly function as interconnected economic regions, Malaysia must confront a larger question.
Does the country possess the fiscal and institutional architecture required to govern such an economy?
For decades, debates on Malaysian federalism have understandably concentrated on constitutional authority, grants, petroleum revenues, development allocations and the distribution of responsibilities between the federal government and the states.
These questions remain important. But redistribution is not the same as integration.
A state can receive larger federal transfers yet remain economically disconnected from the rest of the country. Another can attract billions of ringgit in investment while generating weak linkages with Malaysian suppliers.
A third can record high GDP even though the income generated by its productive assets is not proportionately reflected in household welfare.
The next phase of Malaysian federalism must therefore move beyond asking only who receives what.
It must also ask how the Federation produces together.
Three Pillars of Economic Federalism
Malaysia needs to distinguish between three related concepts. Fiscal federalism concerns revenues, expenditure responsibilities and transfers between governments.
Regional planning concerns infrastructure, transport, housing, environmental management and public services whose economic effects frequently cross administrative boundaries.
Production federalism concerns the relationships connecting industries, workers, suppliers, universities, technologies, logistics and investment across states.
Malaysia already practises elements of all three. The problem is that they are insufficiently connected.
Federal budgets may finance infrastructure without systematically measuring the additional production generated across neighbouring states. Investment incentives may attract factories without adequately determining whether Malaysian suppliers become part of their value chains.
State development strategies may compete for similar industries when regional specialisation would generate greater collective value.
An integrated production economy requires all three pillars to reinforce one another. Fiscal federalism finances capability. Regional planning connects geography. Production federalism connects economic activity.
Transfers Cannot Substitute for Productive Capacity
Fiscal transfers remain essential, especially where poorer or geographically disadvantaged states face higher costs in providing roads, schools, healthcare and basic infrastructure.
Indeed, the government's pre-budget statement 2027 explicitly emphasises narrowing regional development gaps while tailoring development strategies to the strengths and potential of individual states and regions.
But transfers alone cannot eliminate structural economic disparities.
Where industrial linkages are weak, investment limited, skills inadequate and connectivity poor, additional public expenditure can improve services without necessarily transforming the productive structure.
Fiscal redistribution addresses differences in resources. Production policy addresses differences in economic capability. Malaysia needs both.
The objective should therefore be not merely to compensate regions for being weaker, but to use fiscal policy to strengthen their capacity to produce, connect and specialise.
This suggests several reforms.
First, intergovernmental transfers should become increasingly transparent and predictable, with clearer consideration of population, fiscal capacity, infrastructure deficits, geography and the differing costs of delivering comparable public services.
Second, Malaysia should consider Regional Development Compacts between the federal government and participating states around agreed economic objectives.
A northern compact could coordinate semiconductors, advanced manufacturing, water, logistics and talent across Penang, Kedah and adjoining areas.
A southern arrangement could coordinate transport, manufacturing, logistics and housing across increasingly interconnected economic corridors.
Sabah and Sarawak would require arrangements reflecting their distinct constitutional positions, geography and development requirements.
Funding could then support agreed regional outcomes rather than merely collections of isolated projects.
Reward Cooperation, Not Duplication
Federal incentives should also encourage states to cooperate where benefits cross borders.
Suppose Penang and Kedah jointly develop technical training serving semiconductor companies in both states. Or Selangor and Negri Sembilan coordinate industrial transport infrastructure.
Or regional logistics investments in Sabah and Sarawak reduce supply-chain costs across multiple jurisdictions.
Projects producing demonstrable cross-border spillovers should qualify for stronger federal support.
The principle is straightforward: Where economic benefits cross state boundaries, fiscal incentives should encourage governments to behave accordingly. This requires better measurement.
Malaysia's national Input-Output tables already show how industries purchase inputs from and supply outputs to one another. But conventional state GDP cannot adequately show how production in one Malaysian region depends upon another.
Regional Input-Output analysis could. How much of Penang's electronics output depends upon Kedah? How much of Sabah's economy purchases inputs from Peninsular Malaysia?
How much of Sarawak's industrial value remains within Sarawak? Which regions possess strong Malaysian backward linkages, and which rely heavily upon imported intermediate inputs? Where are the largest leakages from domestic production chains?
These are not academic questions. They determine whether an investment creates a wider Malaysian multiplier or remains largely an economic enclave.
The Statistics Department already records interregional merchandise trade between Peninsular Malaysia, Sabah and Sarawak. The statistical foundations therefore exist for progressively deeper analysis.
Regional and ultimately interregional Input-Output frameworks should become regular instruments of national development planning.
Institutions That See Beyond State Borders
Data alone, however, cannot solve coordination failures.
Malaysia should consider permanent regional production councils for its major economic corridors.
These should not constitute another layer of government or assume powers belonging constitutionally to federal or state authorities.
They should be coordinating institutions bringing together relevant ministries, state governments, investment agencies, infrastructure providers, universities and industry.
Their purpose would be practical. Is industrial land being developed without sufficient water or electricity? Are universities training workers without reference to emerging regional demand?
Are ports, railways and highways being planned independently? Are neighbouring states using public resources to duplicate essentially identical industrial clusters?
Regional institutions should identify and resolve precisely these failures.
Federalism as Economic Architecture
Federalism is therefore more than a political arrangement governing the distribution of authority. It is also economic architecture.
Malaysia contains markedly different regional economies. The Klang Valley is services-intensive and highly urbanised. Northern Malaysia contains one of Southeast Asia's important electronics and semiconductor concentrations. Johor is expanding around manufacturing, logistics and integration with Singapore. Sabah and Sarawak possess different combinations of resources, geography, infrastructure constraints and development opportunities.
Uniform policy therefore has limits. But complete decentralisation has limits too.
Malaysia requires national coordination precisely because its regional economies are different.
The objective is not uniformity. It is complementarity.
A factory in Kulim should create opportunities for suppliers in Penang and Perak. A data centre in Johor should generate engineering and service demand elsewhere in Malaysia.
Resource development in Sarawak should build Malaysian technological and supplier capabilities. Infrastructure in Sabah should reduce the cost of participating in national as well as international production networks.
The federation becomes economically stronger when value created in one region generates productive opportunities in another.
State confidence creates ambition. Regional cooperation creates scale. Fiscal architecture creates incentives. Production linkages create multipliers. Institutions make the system durable.
Only then does an even harder question arise. What happens when a state appears prosperous in terms of production, but that prosperity is not proportionately reflected in the incomes of its households?
That is where the next discussion should begin: with the Sarawak paradox, and the critical distinction between the geography of production and the geography of welfare.

Title: When employees are afraid to speak, organisations stop learning
Article:
AT a meeting in a Kuala Lumpur corporate office, the CEO asks, "Any concerns? Nobody speaks. The meeting ends.
In the cafeteria, however there is a roar of activity and discussion among employees, with some openly voicing their views on the problems facing the organisation and what management should do to address them.
Everyone is strident in their views, confidently pontificating on how the lingering problems in the organisation could be resolved.
But all this begs the question as to why there was a deafening silence when the CEO asked if there were any concerns? It is a baffling scenario that can be found in the corporate landscape in Malaysia.
Why is such a scenario prevalent in the Malaysian corporate sector? One reason is the absence of psychological safety- an environment where employees feel able to speak up, ask questions, admit mistakes, challenge ideas and offer suggestions without fear of humiliation or punishment.
This does not mean that an organisation has no accountability. It means people can speak honestly while remaining accountable for their work.
The absence of such an environment can have serious consequences.
Organisations that provide psychological safety for their employees are far more capable of reaching their goals faster and bolstering employee productivity.
Organisations that do not provide such an environment may find that problems remain hidden and decision-makers lack a true sense of what is happening on the ground, as bad news travels slowly upwards.
Managers may therefore have the impression that everything is under control when, in reality, important problems are being kept from them.
The prevailing culture described above depicts what typically takes place where employees say what managers want to hear, which prevents managers from getting a true sense of the problems facing the organisation.
Considering that it would not be beneficial for employees to bring problems to the fore, managers only hear what employees think their bosses want to hear.
In organisations where mistakes are concealed and problems are not discussed, innovation suffers.
It would invariably turn out to be a bureaucratic organisation where employees do not take initiative or responsibility as there are no incentives for doing so.
Decisions become concentrated at the top and are made devoid of the realities of the marketplace. Innovation suffers and employees become less agile in responding to the demands of the marketplace as there is no incentive for them to make decisions.
An organisation that lacks a learning culture and does not inspire confidence among its employees would soon find itself in a tailspin.
Amy Edmondson a reputed Harvard scholar who developed the concept of psychological safety in organisational research said that people perform better when they ask questions, raise concerns, admit mistakes, challenge ideas and ask for help.
Years later, Google conducted a major project entitled "Project Aristotle to understand why some teams performed better than others and the study found that psychological safety was the most important of the five key dynamics associated with effective teams.
Google found that team effectiveness was not simply about putting the smartest or most technically talented people together but how they interacted with each other mattered.
The Google researchers drew on Edmondson's earlier work, demonstrating that the ability of employees to speak up, ask questions and acknowledge mistakes can have a significant bearing on team effectiveness.
There are many examples that Malaysian companies could follow. Pixar is an example of how the creative process depends heavily on people being able to criticise ideas and challenge the work of senior colleagues.
Its Braintrust meetings encourage candid feedback on films in development, allowing creative teams to identify weaknesses before a project reaches the market.
Malaysian managers need to understand that the traditional hierarchical structured organisation would not be able to meet the expectations of customers and markets that are rapidly changing.
To do so, employees must be agile, keep their nose to the grindstone and make decisions swiftly.
If there is no psychological safety, employees would not be willing to take that plunge, leaving the organisation at risk of going downhill in a very short time.
It is therefore important for Malaysian managers to create an environment that inspires confidence among employees to make decisions, take calculated risks and learn from their mistakes without being penalised if organisations here are to navigate a difficult path.
When employees are afraid to speak, silence may give managers the comforting impression that everything is under control.
It may be the clearest warning that something is wrong. An organisation cannot become agile if its people are afraid to speak

With extensive experience in the financial markets and management education, he also served at a prominent think tank. Title: Continued net interest margins compression a risk to lending environment
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: The recent corporate earnings of the banking sector shows continuous net interest margins (NIM) squeeze, as the cost of funds increases as banks compete for deposits – a trend that could take off some of the shine of relatively good results.
If the trend continues, banks might have to increase their interest rates, which might cause borrowers to have to pay higher financing costs on their loans, leading to higher costs of doing business and cost of living.
Tradeview Capital fund manager Neoh Jia Man said that the sector witnessed intensified deposit competition as they looked for funds for their loan growth during the quarter under review which led to NIM compression.
"This means banks will increasingly become more selective in extending credit, which would be detrimental to borrowers and could act as a drag on economic growth as a whole," he told Business Times.
Echoing the view, Bank Muamalat Malaysia Bhd chief economist Dr Mohd Afzanizam Abdul Rashid said banks are obliged to observe their liquidity position such as liquidity coverage ratio and net stable funding ratio.
"This will continue to exert competition for deposits especially at a time when depositors, be it individuals or businesses, would require higher deposit rates as means to attract such customers.
"Some banks which have been effective and efficient in managing their cost of funds would be able to offer competitive deposit rates to the customers," he said.
The issue of NIM squeeze is also highlighted by Hong Leong Investment Bank (HLIB) Research in a note on Sept 4, noting that the sector's margins narrowed by two basis points (bps) quarter-on-quarter (QoQ) and three bps year-on-year (YoY).
Declining NIM is pronounced on Alliance Bank Malaysia Bhd, according to data presented by HLIB Research in the note, although the bank remains having the highest figure among the eight banks under the research firm's coverage, at 2.3 per cent.
Five quarters ago, it was at 2.43 per cent.
Affin Bank Bhd had the lowest NIM during the quarter, at 1.5 per cent, followed by RHB Bank Bhd at 1.8 per cent. Malayan Banking Bhd, Public Bank Bhd, CIMB Group Holdings Bhd and Bank Islam Malaysia Bhd chalked 2.1 per cent NIM during the quarter.
Meanwhile, MBSB Research said that NIM weakness is likely to persist, although steep compression is unlikely.
"Most banks don't expect much recovery in subsequent quarters. Expect deposit competition to remain tight, as long as the high loan demand persists," it said.
On the flipside, the firm said it is more confident in the longer-term NIM outlook, when enough higher-yielding loans have been accumulated to bring visible impact to asset yields.
HIGH NIM BANKS OUTPERFORMS
During the second quarter ended June 30, 2026, banks with higher level of NIM outperforms, such as Alliance Bank, which saw its earnings for the quarter – the first quarter for its financial year ending March 31, 2027 – rose 25 per cent to RM248.32 million.
This is despite its revenue only inched up 2.5 per cent during the quarter, to RM630.93 million.
MBSB Research said in a note on Alliance Bank that the bank's management has revised downward its NIM target, from between 2.28 per cent and 2.35 per cent, to between 2.23 per cent and 2.28 per cent, as the bank focuses on growing NII.
"Regardless, management believes that NIMs are already close to bottoming out. The dilution comes largely from growing a lower-yielding loan mix very quickly. NII accretion, not NIM, is the focus," the research firm noted.
MBSB Research maintained its 'Buy' call on Alliance Bank, with a higher target price of RM6.10, compared with RM5.92 prior to the results. The higher target price reflects Alliance Bank's altered earnings prospects, it said.
Meanwhile, CIMB Securities downgraded Affin Bank to 'Hold' with a target price of RM2.30, after the bank announced its second quarter results ended June 30, 2026, which saw core net profit declines 11.13 per cent YoY to RM127.52 million, weighed down by higher impairment allowances and a lower share of profit from associates.
Its NIM compressed by a marginal two bps during the quarter from the preceding quarter, to 1.52 per cent. According to CIMB Research, the bank's management indicated that NIM would have been higher without the delay in the drawdown of a sizeable high-yielding loan.
CIMB Research's downgrade on Affin Bank is premised on its belief that the risk-reward profile of the bank has skewed to the downside, following two consecutive quarters of elevated provisions.
The research firm noted that the next leg of re-rating requires clearer evidence that credit costs have peaked, retail asset quality is stabilising and net credit cost (NCC) is trending back towards normalised levels below 30 bps.
"Accordingly, valuation now requires proof of ROE delivery rather than execution potential alone," states CIMB Research in an August 17 note.
RISKS TO ASSET QUALITY WITH HIGHER LOAN GROWTH
According to Bank Negara Malaysia's July 2026 banking statistics, system loans expanded 5.6 per cent YoY, a slight uptick from 5.5 per cent YoY in June and 5.4 per cent YoY in July 2025.
The expansion was due to stronger expansion in the non-household segment led by electricity, gas, and water alongside transport and communications.
Malacca Securities head of research Loui Low said that small and medium enterprises (SMEs) drove the uptick in loans in the quarter, coupled with working capital, mortgages and corporate activities.
However, Low opined that higher loan growth also comes with a set of risks.
"The main risks are higher funding costs and potential asset-quality pressure if growth becomes too aggressive. But this is unlikely for the near term," he said.
Meanwhile, Afzanizam said that the non-household sector has been posting strong loan growth of 6.4 per cent in July, well above the industry's loan growth of 5.6 per cent during the same period.
This reflects strong investment activities among private firms that are the key catalyst for the loanable funds.
He added that total loans growth for the household sector was steady at 5.0 per cent growth in July, signaling cautious sentiment surrounding the sector.
"At the same time, choices for households for financing have become widely available from the digital platforms including buy now pay later where it caters to a larger crowd with competitive terms such as no interest charge for a few months. This can be a direct competition for credit cards," he said.
Although the street's view is that NIM compression among banks is likely to continue in the second half of the year, Afzanizam said there is a possibility for the overnight policy rate to normalize by 25 bps next year, which could ease pressure on the margins.
"Otherwise, intense competition for deposit will continue to pose a serious challenge on the deposit rates and hence NIM compression," he said.

Title: Syed Azman faces test of turning HHRG assets into earnings
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: HHRG Bhd's appointment of Tan Sri Syed Azman Syed Ibrahim as executive chairman puts one of Malaysia's better-known entrepreneurs at the helm of a company that needs more than just a new growth story - it needs stronger earnings.
Syed Azman, the founder of Weststar Group, takes over as HHRG continues to grapple with weaker operating performance while pursuing a diversification strategy beyond its traditional biomass and fibre businesses.
His immediate responsibilities include overseeing the group's 60.7-hectare development in Sungai Petani, Kedah, its Kulim land bank and potential new investment opportunities.
The timing is significant.
For the nine months ended June 30 2026, HHRG's revenue fell 22.4 per cent year-on-year to RM70.76 million, while it swung to a loss attributable to shareholders of RM5.92 million from a profit of RM2.24 million previously.
The latest quarter was better, with net profit attributable to shareholders of RM643,000, but revenue still fell 23.4 per cent to RM23.3 million.
HHRG attributed the weaker performance to softer furniture demand, the disposal of its mattress manufacturing business, currency movements, shipment delays and weaker biomass sales caused partly by raw-material shortages.
That leaves Syed Azman with a fairly clear challenge: turn HHRG's asset base into recurring, higher-quality earnings.
An industry observer said his experience could be particularly relevant to the Sungai Petani project, which combines industrial and motorsport-related elements.
His background in automotive, commercial vehicles, aviation, property and construction could help HHRG structure partnerships, attract investors and develop commercial components around the site rather than simply monetising the land.
His broader business network could also be useful in bringing strategic partners into projects that HHRG may not have the balance sheet or expertise to develop alone.
But investors may look beyond the appointment itself.
HHRG's shares closed at 14.5 sen on Sept 4, after touching 16 sen earlier in the week.
The stock had risen sharply from 11.5 sen on Aug 26, but remains well below its 52-week high of 18.5 sen.
The market, therefore, appears to be pricing in expectations of change but has yet to see proof.

Title: Padi farmers demand answers over fertiliser supply delays [WATCH]
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: The investigation into delays in the supply of subsidised fertiliser to padi farmers must determine who was responsible and whether there were weaknesses in the procurement and supply process.
Malaysian Padi Farmers Brotherhood Organisation chairman Abdul Rashid Yob said farmers wanted to know what had happened and who was responsible.
He said farmers had repeatedly raised the fertiliser supply issue with the Agriculture and Food Security Ministry before action was eventually taken.
He added that the investigation should also examine the procurement process, particularly whether decisions made during the evaluation stage were changed when the matter reached the ministry.
"Although there was a procurement board, when the evaluation was carried out there was a merit system, but when it reached the ministry, it changed.
"That is what happened there  and we do not know why. So it needs to be investigated properly," he told the
New Straits Times
.
The issue centres on delays in the supply of Additional Padi Compound Fertiliser 3 (Baja 3) to padi farmers in the Muda Agricultural Development Authority (Mada) area.
The contract of Taveekun Manufacturing Sdn Bhd, which was responsible for supplying Baja 3, was terminated on Aug 27 following the delays.
Agriculture and Food Security Minister Datuk Seri Mohamad Sabu had said Malaysian NPK Fertiliser Sdn Bhd, a subsidiary of Pertubuhan Peladang Kebangsaan, had been appointed to take over the remaining supply to affected farmers.
Delivery of the remaining Baja 3 was to have begun on Sept 3, with the entire process targeted for completion within 10 days.
Mada was also instructed to  monitor the deliveries until the fertiliser reached all affected farmers.
When contacted by the NST, Mada said its current focus was on delivering fertiliser to areas that had yet to receive their supplies.
It was reported that 40,000 of the 60,000 padi farmers in the Mada area had yet to receive Baja 3, raising concerns that the delay could affect this season's padi yields.
Rashid said the delays had placed a  burden on farmers, who had already spent money preparing their land and managing their crops.
"This failure in management was not caused by weather or other factors. It was a human factor and this is something we deeply regret," he said.

Title: Delay in fertiliser distribution to Kedah padi farmers: MACC opens probe
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: The Malaysian Anti-Corruption Commission (MACC) has opened an investigation paper into delays in the distribution of supplementary compound fertiliser, known as Baja 3, to padi farmers in Kedah.
The commission said its Kedah office received a complaint from Pertubuhan Persaudaraan Pesawah Malaysia (Pesawah) on Aug 26 and opened an investigation into the matter.
The probe centres on delays in fertiliser supplies for about 100,000ha of padi-growing areas under the Muda Agricultural Development Authority (Mada).
The supplier involved was appointed by the Agriculture and Food Security Ministry to meet fertiliser requirements in the Mada area.
MACC said its investigation would not only examine possible criminal elements but also any governance weaknesses that may have contributed to the delays.
So far, investigators have recorded a statement from a PeSAWAH witness and obtained several related documents.
The commission said it welcomed the prime minister's concern and call for attention to the issue, adding that it had contacted the Agriculture and Food Security Ministry and Mada to facilitate further investigations.
MACC chief commissioner Datuk Seri Abd Halim Aman, when contacted, confirmed that the investigation was being conducted under Section 18 of the MACC Act 2009.
Section 18 deals with offences involving the submission of documents, statements or accounts containing false or misleading particulars with the intention of deceiving a principal.
An offence under Section 18 is punishable under Section 24 of the Act with imprisonment of up to 20 years and a fine of not less than five times the value of the false or misleading particulars, where these can be valued, or RM10,000, whichever is higher.
Yesterday, Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim instructed the Malaysian Anti-Corruption Commission (MACC) to investigate delays in the distribution of fertiliser to padi farmers in Kedah.
Anwar said the
delays had affected
farmers, who had raised their concerns and submitted memoranda to him.
He said the government needed to determine the cause, including identifying the company entrusted with the distribution and whether it had fulfilled its obligations.
"We have to find out what the cause was. Which company was entrusted with it? Did they fulfil their promise or not? If they did not fulfil it, why was there no action against them?" he said at the closing of the Malaysia Agriculture, Horticulture and Agrotourism Exhibition (Maha) 2026.
Anwar, who is also the finance minister, said enforcement action should be taken where necessary, including bringing those responsible to court or pursuing prosecution.
He said delays in agricultural assistance were particularly serious as farmers and padi growers were already facing challenges, including weather and water-related problems.
In January, the Agriculture and Food Security Ministry
was reported
to be reviewing the subsidised fertiliser supply chain following complaints from farmers that delays had disrupted crop growth and increased their costs.
The ministry said short contract periods had previously caused supply disruptions when contracts expired before new suppliers were appointed. Procurement reforms, including longer contracts, have since been implemented to ensure continuity.

Title: 'Truly scared': Blazes outpace firefighters in Indonesian Borneo
Article:
PONTIANAK: Toiling around the clock, haggard Indonesian firefighters on Borneo island cannot keep up with the blazes devouring landscapes and shrouding communities in a cloying haze.
They are fighting a perilous battle with limited weapons against fires blamed in part on a stronger-than-usual episode of the El Nino climate phenomenon parching Southeast Asia.
Experts also blame climate change, decades of forest degradation and slash-and-burn land clearing practices that have changed the naturally fire-resistant landscape.
"We are exhausted. Sometimes we carry out firefighting until dawn. Sometimes we don't sleep," said Sampe Ritonga, fire chief for Sintang regency.
"Our facilities and infrastructure for firefighting are very limited," he told AFP, standing on the smouldering embers of a peatland fire separated from a residential settlement by a narrow dirt road.
Behind him, veiled by the haze, the sun appeared as an eerie, rust-coloured ball in the brown-grey sky.
Sampe's team only has two 6,000-litre fire engines, and deploys one at a time while the other refills. They also face a shortage of hoses.
The team has fought dozens of fires this month.
With river levels low, "we look for available water in ditches... (and) small rivers", some far from active burn sites, Sampe said.
"So there are difficulties because they have to first carry out firefighting with high intensity, and second look for water," he added.
"With the limitations we have, we try as hard as we can to extinguish the fires and also to reduce the smoke."
Nearby, locals gathered to observe the team's efforts, offering drinking water to first responders.
"There are many houses here, and that is what we have to protect," said Sampe.
- 'CRACKLING SOUND' -
Resident Sutrismi, 47, said she was at home on Saturday when she heard a "crackling sound", looked out of the window and saw smoke rising from the peatland across the road.
Peatland fires, common in the area, generally smoulder and spread under the soil for weeks or months, emitting huge quantities of smoke and only rarely causing surface blazes.
"First thing, I looked for help. I contacted the village head, asked for assistance," Sutrismi told AFP.
"I am scared. Truly scared."
Some 400km away in Pontianak – the capital of West Kalimantan province – people have been breathing foul air for weeks.
The haze can be smelled even indoors in the city of about 700,000 people.
At one point on Sunday, the level of PM2.5 pollution exceeded 500 micrograms per cubic metre, according to IQAir, a Switzerland-based monitor.
That is more than 100 times the World Health Organization's recommended safe limit for airborne particles so small they can enter deep into the lungs and even the bloodstream, with potentially dire consequences for health.
Hundreds of schools have been closed indefinitely in West Kalimantan due to air pollution, with about 200,000 pupils learning from home, according to the education ministry.
The province has also recorded a surge in respiratory ailments.
"We really hope there will be some assistance or grants for us, so we can be faster, more alert and more responsive," said Sampe.
West Kalimantan governor Ria Norsan said the province was doing its best.
"We do not want officers in the field to work with limitations," he said in a statement to AFP.
"Every report regarding shortages of personnel, equipment, water, or other needs must be conveyed immediately so that solutions can be found."
The provincial government has said it has nearly 14,500 fire-fighting personnel out in the field, with nine aircraft available for water-bombing, three for patrols and one for cloud-seeding operations trying to make rain.
- CLIMATE CONNECTION -
Environmental campaigners say rapacious forest and peatland destruction is the root cause of the fires.
"The peat is drained by extractive plantations, monoculture plantations, whether oil palm or pulpwood," Greenpeace Indonesia forest campaigner Belgis Habiba told AFP in Pontianak.
"When the water is drained, the peat dries and becomes flammable."
According to Greenpeace estimates using government data, some 35 million people in Indonesia are exposed to toxic haze.
Smoke from the fires has also affected communities in the neighbouring Malaysian part of Borneo and beyond.
"The haze is massive and everywhere, and it's actually very unfit for people to breathe," Belgis said.
She urged the Indonesian government to declare the fires a national disaster, "so that all resources are mobilised... to build health access for residents, rescue wildlife and so on."
According to the Nusantara Atlas fire tracker, more than 285,000 hectares have burnt in Indonesia so far this year.
Official data show 38,000 hectares have burnt in West Kalimantan.
The current El Nino event, which will last into next year, is likely to be one of the strongest in decades, according to the United Nations.--AFP
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Indonesia shuts main airport, seven others after Anak Krakatoa eruptions
Article:
JAKARTA: About 170,000 passengers were left stranded on Sunday as Indonesia shuttered its main international airport and seven others, cancelling hundreds of flights after Mount Anak Krakatoa spewed a plume of volcanic ash and lava from more than 150 kilometres away.
Mount Anak Krakatoa erupted on Saturday, producing a fountain of lava and booming sounds that could be heard up to a few hundred kilometres away, the geology agency said in a statement.
Two new eruptions were recorded on Sunday, the volcanology agency warned.
Ash from the volcano was detected in the airspace surrounding Soekarno-Hatta International Airport, prompting authorities to suspend operations, the ministry said.
The suspension was extended until 8.59am Monday "due to increased eruptive activity at Mount Anak Krakatoa", the airport authority said in an Instagram post.
Operations were also suspended at seven other airports until 8.59am, authorities said on Instagram. These include the Husein Sastranegara airport in Bandung and Radin Inten II airport near Bandar Lampung on Sumatra, the ministry said.
"To date, 1,558 flights have been delayed at the eight affected airports, with 170,000 passengers stranded," the ministry said in a statement on Sunday.
More than 900 affected flights were to and from the Soekarno-Hatta International Airport, it added.
Several airports in cities including Semarang and Surabaya have been prepared as alternatives for landing, Transportation Minister Dudy Purwagandhi said.
- PASSENGERS SCRAMBLING -
The disruption left some passengers scrambling to find alternative flights.
Henny Yensan, 44, who had hoped to go back to her hometown with her mother, said "everybody was disappointed."
"No one flew into a rage because, after all, this is due to natural disaster," the businesswoman who had to reschedule her flight to Tuesday told AFP.
Samuel Guiberteau, a Danone executive on a business trip to Lombok since Friday, said "nothing is certain for the moment", as he searched for alternative flights back to the capital.
"I had found another flight on Citilink, but it was also cancelled," the 47-year-old told AFP by phone, adding that he had no alternative but to stay in Lombok for the time being.
Volcanic ash also reached the city of Bandar Lampung in the southern tip of Sumatra, blanketing parked cars and roadsides.
"I'm worried it could seriously affect the lungs and cause a lung infection," Andre Bayu Saputra, 25, told AFP on Sunday.
Schools across Jakarta will be closed on Monday as classes move online, the city said in a statement, without specifying how long the measure will be in place.
- HAZARD WARNING -
Anak Krakatoa, which means Child of Krakatoa, sits in a strait that separates the islands of Java and Sumatra.
Ships passing through the strait were asked to increase vigilance for possible disruption to navigation safety due to volcanic activities.
Vessels are prohibited from approaching an exclusion zone of three kilometres radius from the volcano, local port authorities said in a statement.
The volcano has been sporadically active since it emerged from the sea at the beginning of last century in the caldera that formed after the 1883 eruption of Mount Krakatoa.
That disaster was one of the deadliest and most destructive in history with an estimated 35,000 people killed.
Geology agency head Lana Saria said "seismic activity indicates the movement or release of volcanic fluids within the volcanic system."
"However, the timing, magnitude, and nature of the next eruption cannot be precisely predicted," Lana added.
Lana warned against approaching Anak Krakatoa, saying materials ejected from the volcano could endanger those within the exclusion zone.
She said the most recent series of eruptions do not have the potential to trigger a tsunami at this time.
A 2018 tsunami triggered by a collapse of parts of Anak Krakatoa killed 429 people and left thousands displaced.
Indonesia, a Southeast Asian archipelago nation, sits on the Pacific Ring of Fire, where the meeting of continental plates causes high volcanic and seismic activity.--AFP
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Iran threatens greater force if US launches more attacks
Article:
TEHERAN: Iran's top negotiator on Sunday threatened a more forceful response to any further US attacks after Teheran targeted American warships in their latest round of clashes.
The exchanges of fire, which began with US raids last week, come amid a deadlock in the six-month war between the two foes.
Iran has maintained its stranglehold on the strategic Strait of Hormuz while Washington continues a counter-blockade of Iranian ports.
Washington is also seeking to choke Iran's economy, rolling out sanctions on entities with financial links to the Islamic republic in a bid to force it into submission.
Iranian parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, who has acted as chief negotiator in talks to end the war, said Sunday that "the era of proportionate responses has come to an end."
"Any aggression against Iran's interests and security will receive a faster, more intense and more painful response," he added, in a speech carried by state media.
Teheran's top security chief, meanwhile, said Iran would establish a "prohibited zone" near the Strait of Hormuz in coming days.
"This zone will start from the US Navy's blockade line and include areas of the Persian Gulf. Any ship entering this new zone will be placed on the sanctions list" of Iran, Mohsen Rezaei told state TV.
- VESSELS TARGETED -
On Saturday, US Central Command (CENTCOM), which oversees American military operations in the region, said Iran had unsuccessfully fired at two American warships – an aircraft carrier and a destroyer.
In response, the US struck three oil tankers it said were linked to Iran's Revolutionary Guards (IRGC).
Video posted by the military showed large fireballs and billowing flames after projectiles slammed into the ships.
The three vessels were "part of a multibillion-dollar shadow network that funds the IRGC and its regional proxies", CENTCOM said.
Iran quickly retaliated, with the Guards saying their naval forces "targeted three oil tankers on the unauthorised route of the Strait of Hormuz and three vessels affiliated with the child-killing America in other areas."
It warned ships not to attempt to transit the key trade waterway via routes not approved by Teheran.
Early on Sunday Iran's Guards also said they attacked a US naval drone trying to enter the strait, according to a statement carried by state television.
CENTCOM spokesman Captain Tim Hawkins, however, called the claim "a complete lie."
- 'CLINGING ON TO POWER' -
CENTCOM commander Admiral Brad Cooper had said after the exchange of strikes: "If you shoot at two of our ships, we will impose an even higher economic cost – taking out three of yours."
The Iranian foreign ministry condemned the attacks on its oil tankers as "illegal and aggressive actions."
The administration of US President Donald Trump has tried to downplay the significance of the six-month conflict, which has proven increasingly unpopular at home as midterm elections near.
US Vice President JD Vance has gone so far as to say that he "wouldn't call it a war."
Trump reiterated that view on Friday, calling the war "small potatoes" for Washington.
Iranian officials have maintained their defiant tone, but US Energy Secretary Chris Wright told ABC's "This Week" programme on Sunday that Iran was "doing everything they can to cling on to something."
"They know their nuclear programme's coming to an end. Their navy has come to an end. Their air force has come to an end. They're clinging on to power," he said.
A fragile ceasefire between the two sides collapsed in July after attacks on commercial ships in the Hormuz strait, through which one-fifth of world oil supplies previously flowed.
Trump has in recent weeks repeatedly threatened to claim sovereignty over the strait, even posting a map showing it as "new US territory."
Vance has insisted the US will not reopen talks with Iran until it ends attacks on commercial shipping in the strait.--AFP
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Five dead, five injured after Amazon cargo plane overshoots Miami runway
Article:
MIAMI: At least five people were killed when an Amazon cargo plane overshot a runway after it landed Sunday at Miami International Airport, crashed into vehicles and caught fire, officials said.
Miami-Dade County fire chief Ray Jadallah told reporters that in addition to five fatalities, three people were transported to trauma centres "in critical condition" and two more were treated at a local hospital.
"The airplane did strike a couple of vehicles," which left "a couple of victims that were actually trapped in the vehicles," Jadallah said.
"A complex extrication with our technical rescue team" was needed, "including a search and rescue of the pilot and co-pilot that were trapped in this aircraft."
Jadallah did not clarify whether the pilot or co-pilot survived, and officials declined to answer questions after brief statements were made.
Video showed thick smoke billowing from the blue and white Boeing 767 that had arrived around 2pm (1800 GMT) from Puerto Rico, as fire trucks raced to the scene.
The plane operating as Prime Air Flight 7598 caught fire as a result of the "crash," fire officials said.
"A total of 60 fire apparatuses arrived, just short, just shy of 200 men and women from Miami-Dade Fire Rescue, to begin the actual search and rescue and firefighting," Jadallah said.
"The actual cause of the incident will be determined by the FAA and the NTSB," he added, referring to the Federal Aviation Administration and National Transportation Safety Board.
The NTSB said in an X post on Sunday the B-767-300 cargo airplane was flying into Miami from San Juan, Puerto Rico and they have "launched a go team to investigate Sunday's runway excursion accident."
The airport closed all runways and taxiways because of the incident and posted an update to its website Sunday evening that travelers should check directly with their airline before heading to the airport.
Amazon put out a statement saying the aircraft "experienced an incident while attempting to land." It did not say if anyone was hurt or killed.
"This is a fast-moving situation and we're still gathering details. We're working closely with local authorities and officials to understand exactly what happened," Amazon spokesperson Kelly Nantel said in the statement.
Miami Sheriff Rosie Cordero-Stutz told reporters Sunday that her officers encountered a "really tragic scene," but there was "no apparent threat to public safety." -AFP

OSLO: The uncrewed Spectrum rocket was the first commercial flight to reach orbit from continental Europe, where several nations have said they want a share of a growing market for space missions.
"We're in orbit! And just made European history," Isar said in a post on the social media platform X.
The event was a breakthrough for the European launch industry, giving the continent better access to space, Norway's Industry and Commerce Minister Cecilie Myrseth said in a statement.
"The fact that we can now launch satellites from Andoeya strengthens Norwegian and European security in the turbulent times we live in."
Blasting off from Norway's Arctic Andoeya Spaceport, Spectrum — designed for small and medium-sized payloads —  carried five small satellites, as well as an in-flight technological experiment, according to Isar.
It was Isar's second launch, coming 18 months after the company's first rocket plunged into the sea and exploded in a fiery spectacle shortly after takeoff from the same site. No one was injured at the time.
Saturday's launch was intended as "both the vehicle's qualification mission and its first flight carrying payload", the Bavarian company has said.
Global players in the satellite launch market include Elon Musk's SpaceX, which launches from the US, and French ArianeGroup, a joint venture between Airbus and Safran that uses a spaceport in South America's French Guiana.
Sweden, with its Esrange launch site and Britain, with its SaxaVord Spaceport in the Scottish Shetland Islands, are the nearest rivals to the Norwegian site.
Isar last week said it had secured about 200 million euros from the European Space Agency to help fund development of new rockets and expand its testing and launch infrastructure.
The German company is also developing a second launch site in Canada.

Title: Helping Malaysians invest smarter
Article:
Your browser does not support the audio element.
KUALA LUMPUR: The Securities Commission (SC) and Bursa Malaysia Bhd have launched the inaugural InvestSmart x Bursa Marketplace Fair 2026 to promote investor education and protect investors against scams.
The two-day event brings together the SC and Bursa Malaysia's flagship investor engagement platforms for the first time.
It was officiated by Treasury secretary-general Tan Sri Johan Mahmood Merican.
The collaboration highlights the importance of investor education and financial literacy as more Malaysians explore a wider range of investment products, digital platforms and information sources.
The SC said the collaboration reflects a shared commitment by both organisations to strengthen investor education.
By bringing together the two flagship investor engagement platforms, both organisations aim to reach more people and promote informed investing and investor protection.
The event combines investor education, market insights and practical guidance to help participants evaluate investment opportunities, understand risks and spot potential scams.
SC chairman Datuk Mohammad Faiz Azmi said broader participation in the capital market remains essential to support a financially resilient and inclusive society.
"For many Malaysians, concerns about fraud and limited access to reliable investment information remain barriers to investing.
"This collaboration aims to improve access to trusted financial information and digital investment tools, empowering more Malaysians to invest with confidence and take greater charge of their long-term financial wellbeing."
Faiz said the SC remains committed to strengthening investor education and financial literacy through strategic partnerships, including with the National Scam Response Centre and the Financial Education Network.
From January to July 2026, the SC received 1,272 enquiries, or 70.6 per cent of cases, from people seeking to verify investment opportunities before investing, compared with 530 complaints, or 29.4 per cent, from scam victims.
The higher proportion of enquiries points to greater awareness of the need to conduct due diligence before investing.
Bursa Malaysia chief executive officer Datuk Fad'l Mohamed said the local capital market offers a wide range of opportunities, while growing participation, particularly among younger investors, reflects greater interest in building financial resilience.
"By bringing market experts, listed companies and financial institutions under one roof, we hope to make it easier for more Malaysians to explore investment opportunities, build their knowledge and take the next step from saving to investing.
"This supports our broader goal of fostering a vibrant and inclusive capital market that enables more Malaysians to participate in and benefit from the nation's economic growth."
Retail participation in the capital market continues to grow, with more than 342,000 new Central Depository System (CDS) accounts opened in the first six months of 2026, up about 24 per cent from the same period last year.
Around 60 per cent of the new accounts were opened by investors aged 35 and under, showing growing participation among younger Malaysians.
Retail investors also accounted for between 27 per cent and 33 per cent of total trading activity over the past three years.
The fair brings together up to 40 exhibitors, giving visitors access to market experts, financial intermediaries, regulators, publicly listed companies, crowdfunding platforms and other industry practitioners.

Title: Jakarta-bound passengers advised to check flights
Article:
Your browser does not support the audio element.
PUTRAJAYA: Passengers travelling to Jakarta have been advised to check their flight status before heading to the airport, after the Soekarno-Hatta International Airport was temporarily closed due to volcanic ash from Mount Anak Krakatau.
Malaysia Airports Holdings Bhd urged passengers to contact their respective airlines for the latest flight status, adding that updates on operations and the airport's reopening would be announced accordingly.
Indonesia's Directorate-General of Civil Aviation said the closure was issued under Notice to Airmen A3341/26 yesterday.
Civil aviation director-general Lukman F. Laisa said tests confirmed the presence of volcanic ash at the airport.
Up to 10pm on Saturday, 33 flights at Soekarno-Hatta International Airport had been affected. International services recorded 16 cancellations, seven delays and five rescheduled flights.
Affected routes included flights to and from Singapore, Hong Kong, Sydney, Seoul/Incheon, Doha, Amsterdam and Kuala Lumpur.
Batik Air said affected passengers could reschedule to the next available flight or request a refund.
AirAsia said the situation remained fluid and advised passengers travelling to and from affected destinations to check their latest flight status before heading to the airport.
Anak Krakatau has been erupting since Sept 4, with ash plumes detected thousands of metres in the air in some areas.
The volcano lies between Java and Sumatra along the Pacific "Ring of Fire", where earthquakes and volcanic eruptions are frequent.
Bernama reported that Malaysia Airlines and Batik Air had cancelled a total of 20 flights between Malaysia and Jakarta.
In a post on X, Malaysia Airlines said it had cancelled 12 flights between Kuala Lumpur and Jakarta.
Batik Air said it had cancelled eight flights.
